sentences.text: The only known species, Concornis lacustris, is represented by a single fairly complete skeleton that lacks the skull, neck, and pygostyle. This small bird measured approximately 13 centimeters in length and possessed no tail.
Estimates for its size vary slightly, with a wingspan of 34 centimeters and a weight ranging between 70 and 100 grams.
Although the skull is missing, the animal almost certainly had teeth in a snout rather than a beak. It also featured a large hallux, a toe trait generally absent in terrestrial birds.
The holotype specimen MCCM-LH-1184 was first described in 1992 while still partially covered in sandstone.
A 2018 study analyzed the creature's proportions to determine that it likely engaged in bounding flight, a pattern seen in modern small birds.

Fossils of Concornis are found in the Calizas de La Huérgina Formation at Las Hoyas, Cuenca province, Spain. The animal lived during the late Barremian age of the early Cretaceous, approximately 125 million years ago.

Studies indicate Concornis could perform continuous flapping flight but was likely unable to glide due to its high body mass to wingspan ratio. Its legs were fairly long with a large hallux, neither specialized for perching nor for running.
Research suggests Concornis likely engaged in bounding flight, a pattern seen in modern small birds.
A 2008 analysis placed Concornis in the family Avisauridae based on features of the tibiotarsus. Under this classification, it is the oldest and most complete member of the family.

A relationship with Sinornis and Cathayornis has been suggested based on a unique Y-shaped sternum with deep notches. Despite its early age, Concornis appears to be a fairly derived member of Enantiornithes.
The time range for Concornis is the Barremian, from 125.77 to 121.4 million years ago.

It is unknown whether Concornis had an alula, though it is likely present based on other enantiornitheans. Concornis is sometimes considered a member of Enantiornithiformes and related to Enantiornis. A cladistic analysis placed Concornis in Cathayornithiformes, grouping it with Sinornis and surprisingly with Neuquenornis volans, which belongs to a different lineage of Euenantiornithes.
